Summary
The paper introduces Action Schema Networks (ASNets), a graph-convolutional neural-network architecture that overcomes several long-standing problems in learning for automated planning.  Core risks addressed are (1) poor cross-instance generalisation of existing planners, (2) the opacity of neural policies, (3) ASNet’s own receptive-field and scalability limits, and (4) language-coverage gaps.  The authors propose weight-sharing by action-schema, position-aware pooling, skip connections, heuristic inputs, sparsity-inducing regularisation, improved grounding, and future architectural extensions.  Extensive experiments validate many of these design choices.  The knowledge fabric below links every risk to concrete, life-cycle-labelled interventions through the exact mechanisms, findings and design features stated in the paper.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[83]
– Fabric connects all stated risks to every intervention mentioned in the source.  
– Node names follow required granularity; edges respect direction and type rules.  
– Remaining uncertainty: some edges necessarily rely on moderate inference when authors only hint at future work (quantifier support, goal-processing network).  

Inference strategy justification
Moderate inference (confidence 2) was applied only when the paper speaks about “future work”.  Otherwise nodes and edges rely on explicit statements or quantitative results (confidence 3-4).

Extraction completeness
24 nodes (~15/5000 words) capture every distinct mechanism, finding, limitation and intervention that forms a reasoning path from a top-level risk to an actionable mitigation.

Key limitations
1. The source is itself a methods paper, so highest-level “risks” are research/engineering limitations, not existential-safety risks.  
2. Inter-paper node-name consistency was approximated with best judgement; large-scale corpus alignment may still merge or split some concepts.
